extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of ancient history and classical chronology (historians, chronologers, classicists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and principles for reconstructing and correcting ancient chronologies and calendars (Greek, Roman, Egyptian, Near Eastern), including how to count reigns, generations, Olympiads, and lunisolar months. Emphasises realistic averages, synchronisms, and use of primary local records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility cutoff for pre-literate claims
rubrics_metrics.description: "And things said to be done above one or two hundred years before the use of letters, are of little credit."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat asserted events placed more than ~100–200 years before the adoption of writing in a region with strong scepticism unless supported by independent, contemporary evidence. Avoid accepting long verbal traditions as firm chronological data when they predate local literacy by centuries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate reign-lengths with generational lengths (Egyptian practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Egyptians reckoned the Reigns of Kings equipollent to Generations of men, and three Generations to an hundred years; Greek chronologers followed this and thereby inflated reign-lengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the Egyptian/ancient tendency to treat each royal reign as a full generational unit (e.g., ~33–40 years). Instead, treat such equality as a suspect technical convention that can produce systematic overestimation of chronological spans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use realistic average reign length for kings (~18–20 years)
rubrics_metrics.description: "For by the ordinary course of nature Kings Reign, one with another, about eighteen or twenty years a-piece... eighteen or twenty years is a medium."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When estimating the length of a sequence of kings (absent specific evidence), use an average of c.18–20 years per reign rather than inflated ancient averages (30–46). Adjust for contexts (e.g., turbulent/elective polities where shorter reigns are common). Example: recomputing Spartan king-lists by 18–20 years greatly shortens earlier Greek chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose generation length based on context (≈28–34 years)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Generations from father to son, may be reckoned one with another at about 33 or 34 years... but if the reckoning proceed by the eldest sons, they are shorter... three of them may be reckoned at about 75 or 80 years... we may reckon about 28 or at the most about 30 years to a Generation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ~33–34 years per generation for average father-to-son reckoning; use shorter values (≈28–30) where genealogies follow principal/eldest lines or when explicit familial succession suggests shorter intervals. Explicitly state which convention is applied and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer anchoring with synchronisms (Olympiads, named battles, well-dated rulers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The text repeatedly uses Olympiad counts, battles (Thermopylae), named reigns and their positions (e.g., Leonidas at the sixth year of Xerxes) to place events and to recalculate earlier dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor relative counts to securely datable synchronisms (Olympiads, solar/lunar festival records, well-attested foreign rulers, known destructions) wherever possible. Use these fixed points to test and correct sequences derived from king- or generation-counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject artificial additions (feigned Olympiads or invented reigns)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Artificial Chronologers, have made Lycurgus... and, to help out the Hypothesis, they have feigned twenty eight Olympiads older than the first Olympiad."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sceptical of chronologies that depend on apparently fabricated or gratuitously inserted intervals (extra Olympiads, spurious long reigns). Prefer parsimonious reconstructions grounded in evidence; flag where previous compilers appear to have invented spacing to reconcile narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct inflated pre-Persian Greek chronology by shortening (approx. two-to-one)
rubrics_metrics.description: "That Chronology is to be rectified, by shortening the times which preceded the death of Cyrus, in the proportion of almost two to one; for the times which follow the death of Cyrus are not much amiss."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing traditional Greek chronologies that predate Cyrus, consider reducing the summed intervals substantially (roughly halving where obvious inflation exists) to better match realistic reign/generation averages and synchronisms. Explicitly document the factor applied and the rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use native/local archival evidence where available (Carthage, Tyre, Cyprus)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Romans conquered the Carthaginians, the Archives of Carthage came into their hands... if the Romans... had these things from the records of Carthage, Cyprus, or Tyre...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give strong weight to indigenous documentary or inscriptional records and local archival material when available; these can correct or supersede later Greek or Roman chronological traditions. Cite the local source and assess its internal consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruct ancient calendars as lunisolar with intercalation cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: "The ancient Calendar year of the Greeks consisted therefore of twelve Lunar months, and every month of thirty days... To the twelve Lunar months the ancient Greeks added a thirteenth, every other year... they omitted an intercalary month once in eight years... the Octaeteris... Meton found out the Cycle of intercaling seven months in nineteen years."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model ancient calendars as lunisolar: months tied to lunar phases (≈29–30 days), years adjusted to solar seasons by intercalary months (octaeteris, later Metonic corrections). When converting ancient dates to Julian/solar dates, explicitly account for intercalation rules known/claimed for the culture and period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow for 360-day administrative counts and later corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: "The year of 360 days was the year, to the end of which they added five days." (Egyptians/Early calendars)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that some ancient sources or ritual contexts used a 360-day 'administrative' year with extra days appended; account for such conventions when reconciling ritual festival lists, priestly records, or statue counts with astronomical/solar years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for differing start-of-year conventions across peoples
rubrics_metrics.description: Some begin the year upon the Summer Solstice (Attica); or upon the Autumnal Equinox (Asia); or in Winter (Romans); or about the Vernal Equinox (Arabians and People of Damascus). The month began, according to some, upon the Full Moon, or upon the New.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aligning calendars and festival dates between cultures, explicitly model the local new-year convention (solstice/equinox/winter/vernal) and local month-start rule (new moon vs full moon). Failure to account for differing year starts can shift seasonal attributions of events by months or even seasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use festival and sacrificial timing to fix seasonal placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Sacrifices (vernal, æstivum) and festival timings were tied to solar seasons; Greeks scheduled years to keep the same seasonal sacrifices to gods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit fixed seasonal festivals and sacrificial calendars (e.g., Passover at full moon of Abib, Pythic/Olympic games) as anchors tying lunar month counts to solar seasons. This helps determine whether a given lunisolar scheme used intercalation to keep festivals in their proper seasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate intervals by multiplying counted reigns/generations by realistic means
rubrics_metrics.description: The author repeatedly demonstrates computing years by multiplying the number of kings/generations by an assumed average (e.g., ten kings × 20 years = 200 years), and contrasts this with inflated ancient totals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When faced with a list of N successive rulers or generations, estimate the elapsed time by multiplying by a justified average (e.g., ~18–20 years per reign; ~28–34 years per generation), and present uncertainty ranges. Use known short reigns, depositions, elective successions to adjust the average down where applicable; compare result to independent synchronisms.
